references.text: Refers to the Israelites leaving in the month of Abib, confirming that this month was set as the first month of the year.
Mentions the Feast of Unleavened Bread in the month of Abib when the Israelites left Egypt, affirming this month's significance as the beginning of the year.
Repeats the command to observe the Feast of Unleavened Bread in the month of Abib, the appointed time when they left Egypt.
Command to keep Passover in the month of Abib, because it was in this month that the Lord brought the people out of Egypt.
The Israelites are commanded to keep Passover in the first month, confirming the arrangement from Exodus 12:2.
Passover is to be kept on the fourteenth day of the first month, showing that this month was counted as the first of the year.
The book of Esther mentions the first month (Nisan), reflecting the Jewish calendar tradition based on this ordinance.
Ezekiel describes the Passover celebration on the fourteenth day of the first month, in agreement with the rule that this month is the beginning of the year.
The Lord's Passover is to be kept on the fourteenth day of the first month, confirming the calendar system established in Exodus 12:2.

Both verses define a historical turning point where 'the first day of the first month' marks the start of a new chapter: first the deliverance from Egypt, then the dedication of God's presence in the tabernacle.
Direct continuation within the same chapter; 12:2 sets the time (the first month) while 12:18 defines the action (the Feast of Unleavened Bread) within this timeframe.
Prophetic parallel: Ezekiel uses the same time reference to dedicate the new temple, highlighting the theological significance of 'the first day' as a moment of God's cleansing and presence.
Confirms the unchanging timeframe for Passover in 'the first month' from Exodus to the prophetic future temple.
